It feels like I'm always worrying about it now.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that your appearance is truly abnormal or flawed, or do you recognize that your concerns about your appearance might be exaggerated or not based in reality?\n\nPatient: I truly believe my appearance is flawed, because to me, my nose looks genuinely crooked and swollen and my face looks completely uneven. Even when my family tries to reassure me, I can't help but feel like these flaws are completely real. I feel like they are so obvious that everyone else can see them immediately, especially under those bright store lights.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever sought a professional opinion, such as from a dermatologist or plastic surgeon, about the flaws you perceive in your appearance, and if so, what was their assessment?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't ever seen a dermatologist or a plastic surgeon for this. I've mostly just tried to fix it myself using makeup, or I just avoid going out at all when it feels too bad.\n\nDoctor: If a dermatologist or plastic surgeon were to examine you and tell you that your appearance is within the normal range and there's nothing significantly flawed about your face, would you be able to accept their professional assessment, or do you think you would still be convinced that there's something wrong with your appearance?\n\nPatient: I haven't really thought about consulting a specialist like a plastic surgeon or dermatologist. I'm honestly not sure if I would be able to believe them, because I feel so strongly that my face looks wrong. Even if they told me it was fine, I think I would still see the flaws when I look in the mirror.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your concerns about your appearance would decrease if you were to receive reassurance from multiple people, including professionals, that your appearance is normal, or would your concerns persist despite their reassurances?\n\nPatient: I already ask my little sister for reassurance constantly, but it never stops me from getting stuck in that loop and being late. Because I can see how crooked and swollen my nose is so clearly in the mirror, I don't think even a professional's reassurance would change how I feel. My concerns would definitely persist because the flaws are just too obvious to me.\n\nDoctor: Do you experience any other recurring, intrusive thoughts or compulsions to perform specific rituals outside of those related to your appearance, such as excessive cleaning, ordering, or counting?\n\nPatient: No, I don't experience anything like that. I've never had any urges to do things like excessive cleaning, ordering, or counting. My worries and rituals are strictly focused on my appearance and how my face looks.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how much time you spend each day thinking about your appearance or performing rituals to check or fix how you look?\n\nPatient: It takes up a massive portion of my day—honestly, it feels like pretty much all day because my brain constantly circles back to my face even when I'm working or talking to my mom. Before my shifts, I can spend hours stuck in that loop of bouncing between the mirror, taking selfies, and redoing my makeup. It takes so much time that I am repeatedly late for work because I just can't stop.\n\nDoctor: If you were to cover your mirrors at home and avoid taking selfies for a period, such as a week, do you think your concerns about your appearance would decrease, or would they persist even without the constant visual reminders?\n\nPatient: I think my worries would actually get worse because even without a mirror, my mind constantly circles back to how crooked and swollen my nose looks throughout the day. Not being able to check would make me feel completely out of control and terrified of what other people are seeing when they look at me."

I just can't bring myself to leave the house until it looks \"less messed up,\" which is why I end up so late.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel a strong sense of anxiety or fear if you can't complete these checking and fixing rituals before leaving the house?\n\nPatient: Yes, the anxiety and pressure are completely overwhelming, to the point where I feel physically frozen and unable to leave the house. I just feel like I absolutely cannot face the customers or the store cameras until I finish checking and feel like my face looks \"less messed up.\"\n\nDoctor: Do you experience significant distress or anxiety related to your appearance in situations outside of work, such as social gatherings or everyday activities, or is it primarily focused on your work shifts?\n\nPatient: Yes, it definitely affects my life outside of work too. I’ve stopped going out with my friends and refuse to let anyone take photos of me because I’m so ashamed of how I look. Even when I'm just at home trying to talk to my mom or sister, I can't stop obsessing over how crooked and swollen my nose and face look.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a specific situation where you felt your appearance was acceptable, or has there ever been a time when you didn't worry about how you looked?\n\nPatient: Honestly, I can't really think of a time when I felt like my appearance was acceptable. These insecurities have been there since my teenage years, but lately, they've just become so much more constant and intense. It feels like I'm always worrying about it now.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that your appearance is truly abnormal or flawed, or do you recognize that your concerns about your appearance might be exaggerated or not based in reality?\n\nPatient: I truly believe my appearance is flawed, because to me, my nose looks genuinely crooked and swollen and my face looks completely uneven. Even when my family tries to reassure me, I can't help but feel like these flaws are completely real. I feel like they are so obvious that everyone else can see them immediately, especially under those bright store lights.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever sought a professional opinion, such as from a dermatologist or plastic surgeon, about the flaws you perceive in your appearance, and if so, what was their assessment?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't ever seen a dermatologist or a plastic surgeon for this. I've mostly just tried to fix it myself using makeup, or I just avoid going out at all when it feels too bad.\n\nDoctor: If a dermatologist or plastic surgeon were to examine you and tell you that your appearance is within the normal range and there's nothing significantly flawed about your face, would you be able to accept their professional assessment, or do you think you would still be convinced that there's something wrong with your appearance?\n\nPatient: I haven't really thought about consulting a specialist like a plastic surgeon or dermatologist. I'm honestly not sure if I would be able to believe them, because I feel so strongly that my face looks wrong. Even if they told me it was fine, I think I would still see the flaws when I look in the mirror.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your concerns about your appearance would decrease if you were to receive reassurance from multiple people, including professionals, that your appearance is normal, or would your concerns persist despite their reassurances?\n\nPatient: I already ask my little sister for reassurance constantly, but it never stops me from getting stuck in that loop and being late. My concerns would definitely persist because the flaws are just too obvious to me.\n\nDoctor: Do you experience any other recurring, intrusive thoughts or compulsions to perform specific rituals outside of those related to your appearance, such as excessive cleaning, ordering, or counting?\n\nPatient: No, I don't experience anything like that. I've never had any urges to do things like excessive cleaning, ordering, or counting. My worries and rituals are strictly focused on my appearance and how my face looks.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how much time you spend each day thinking about your appearance or performing rituals to check or fix how you look?\n\nPatient: It takes up a massive portion of my day—honestly, it feels like pretty much all day because my brain constantly circles back to my face even when I'm working or talking to my mom. Before my shifts, I can spend hours stuck in that loop of bouncing between the mirror, taking selfies, and redoing my makeup. It takes so much time that I am repeatedly late for work because I just can't stop.\n\nDoctor: If you were to cover your mirrors at home and avoid taking selfies for a period, such as a week, do you think your concerns about your appearance would decrease, or would they persist even without the constant visual reminders?\n\nPatient: I think my worries would actually get worse because even without a mirror, my mind constantly circles back to how crooked and swollen my nose looks throughout the day. Not being able to check would make me feel completely out of control and terrified of what other people are seeing when they look at me.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that others notice the flaws in your appearance as readily as you do, or do you think they might not see them as clearly as you see them?\n\nPatient: I absolutely believe everyone notices it immediately. I constantly picture how awful my face looks to other people, especially under the bright store lights and security cameras at work. It feels like everyone can see that something is completely wrong with me the second they look up.\n\nDoctor: If you were to see a picture of yourself from a few years ago, when you felt less anxious about your appearance, would you still perceive the same flaws in that picture, or do you think your perception of those flaws has changed over time?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, to be honest, because I try to completely avoid looking at old photos of myself. I haven't really thought about how my perception might have changed over time, since I'm just so focused on how bad it feels right now.\n\nDoctor: If you were to see a picture of yourself that someone else took, without you being able to check or prepare your appearance beforehand, do you think the flaws you perceive would be as noticeable to you as they are when you're checking yourself in the mirror?\n\nPatient: Unprepared photos are actually my absolute worst nightmare, which is why I completely avoid letting anyone take pictures of me. I just feel like I absolutely cannot face the customers or the store cameras until I finish checking and feel like my face looks \"less messed up.\"\n\nDoctor: Do you experience significant distress or anxiety related to your appearance in situations outside of work, such as social gatherings or everyday activities, or is it primarily focused on your work shifts?\n\nPatient: Yes, it definitely affects my life outside of work too. I’ve stopped going out with my friends and refuse to let anyone take photos of me because I’m so ashamed of how I look. Even when I'm just at home trying to talk to my mom or sister, I can't stop obsessing over how crooked and swollen my nose and face look.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a specific situation where you felt your appearance was acceptable, or has there ever been a time when you didn't worry about how you looked?\n\nPatient: Honestly, I can't really think of a time when I felt like my appearance was acceptable. It feels like I'm always worrying about it now.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that your appearance is truly abnormal or flawed, or do you recognize that your concerns about your appearance might be exaggerated or not based in reality?\n\nPatient: I truly believe my appearance is flawed, because to me, my nose looks genuinely crooked and swollen and my face looks completely uneven. I feel like they are so obvious that everyone else can see them immediately, especially under those bright store lights.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever sought a professional opinion, such as from a dermatologist or plastic surgeon, about the flaws you perceive in your appearance, and if so, what was their assessment?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't ever seen a dermatologist or a plastic surgeon for this. My worries and rituals are strictly focused on my appearance and how my face looks.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how much time you spend each day thinking about your appearance or performing rituals to check or fix how you look?\n\nPatient: It takes up a massive portion of my day—honestly, it feels like pretty much all day because my brain constantly circles back to my face even when I'm working or talking to my mom. I constantly picture how awful my face looks to other people, especially under the bright store lights and security cameras at work. It feels like everyone can see that something is completely wrong with me the second they look up.\n\nDoctor: If you were to see a picture of yourself from a few years ago, when you felt less anxious about your appearance, would you still perceive the same flaws in that picture, or do you think your perception of those flaws has changed over time?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, to be honest, because I try to completely avoid looking at old photos of myself. I haven't really thought about how my perception might have changed over time, since I'm just so focused on how bad it feels right now.\n\nDoctor: If you were to see a picture of yourself that someone else took, without you being able to check or prepare your appearance beforehand, do you think the flaws you perceive would be as noticeable to you as they are when you're checking yourself in the mirror?\n\nPatient: Unprepared photos are actually my absolute worst nightmare, which is why I completely avoid letting anyone take pictures of me. When I do see photos of myself, like from work events, I scrutinize them intensely because my crooked nose and uneven face look incredibly obvious and terrible, especially since I couldn't control the angle or lighting.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever experience any moments where you are able to forget about or not think about your appearance, or is it a constant preoccupation for you throughout the day?\n\nPatient: No, it is a constant preoccupation pretty much all day long. Even when I'm trying to focus on ringing up customers at work or talking to my mom, my mind just keeps circling back to how crooked and swollen my nose looks and how uneven my face is. I constantly worry about how awful it must look to everyone under those bright store lights and security cameras.\n\nDoctor: If you were to watch a video of yourself from an outside perspective, without being able to control the camera angles or editing, do you think you would still perceive the same level of flaws in your appearance as you do when you're checking yourself in the mirror?\n\nPatient: Yes, I would definitely see the same flaws, and they would probably look even worse to me. That is actually one of my biggest fears, especially with the security cameras at work under those bright lights where I can't control the angle. I constantly worry about how crooked and swollen my nose or how uneven my face must look in those videos.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your preoccupation with your appearance and the rituals you perform to check and fix it are unreasonable or excessive, or do you believe they are justified given the flaws you perceive in your appearance?\n\nPatient: It is incredibly exhausting and frustrating to get stuck in these loops and constantly be late, but I genuinely believe the flaws on my face, like my crooked nose and uneven features, are very real and obvious. Because these flaws feel so unacceptable and noticeable to everyone, I feel completely justified and compelled to try to fix them before I can leave the house, even if it seems excessive to other people.\n\nDoctor: If you were to accept that your appearance is within the normal range, as a professional might assess, would you still feel the need to perform these checking and fixing rituals, or would that change your behavior?"

Reply naturally in English as the Patient to the last Doctor utterance.\nAnswer only the question, in 2–3 sentences maximum.\n\n[Dialogue]\nDoctor: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see us today?\n\nPatient: I spend so long checking and fixing how I look before work that I’m missing shifts and still feel like my face looks completely wrong. I'm just really stressed out because it's starting to ruin my job, and I don't know how to make it stop.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about what you mean by 'checking and fixing' your appearance, and are there any specific rituals or behaviors you feel compelled to repeat?\n\nPatient: Before every shift, I get stuck in this loop where I'm constantly running between the bathroom mirror and my phone, taking tons of selfies and zooming in to check my nose and jaw. I'll repeatedly redo my makeup and hair, and keep asking my little sister if I look weird. I just can't bring myself to leave the house until it looks \"less messed up,\" which is why I end up so late.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel a strong sense of anxiety or fear if you can't complete these checking and fixing rituals before leaving the house?\n\nPatient: Yes, the anxiety and pressure are completely overwhelming, to the point where I feel physically frozen and unable to leave the house. I just feel like I absolutely cannot face the customers or the store cameras until I finish checking and feel like my face looks \"less messed up.\"\n\nDoctor: Do you experience significant distress or anxiety related to your appearance in situations outside of work, such as social gatherings or everyday activities, or is it primarily focused on your work shifts?\n\nPatient: Yes, it definitely affects my life outside of work too. I’ve stopped going out with my friends and refuse to let anyone take photos of me because I’m so ashamed of how I look. Even when I'm just at home trying to talk to my mom or sister, I can't stop obsessing over how crooked and swollen my nose and face look.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a specific situation where you felt your appearance was acceptable, or has there ever been a time when you didn't worry about how you looked?\n\nPatient: Honestly, I can't really think of a time when I felt like my appearance was acceptable. These insecurities have been there since my teenage years, but lately, they've just become so much more constant and intense. It feels like I'm always worrying about it now.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that your appearance is truly abnormal or flawed, or do you recognize that your concerns about your appearance might be exaggerated or not based in reality?\n\nPatient: I truly believe my appearance is flawed, because to me, my nose looks genuinely crooked and swollen and my face looks completely uneven. Even when my family tries to reassure me, I can't help but feel like these flaws are completely real. I feel like they are so obvious that everyone else can see them immediately, especially under those bright store lights.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever sought a professional opinion, such as from a dermatologist or plastic surgeon, about the flaws you perceive in your appearance, and if so, what was their assessment?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't ever seen a dermatologist or a plastic surgeon for this. I've mostly just tried to fix it myself using makeup, or I just avoid going out at all when it feels too bad.\n\nDoctor: If a dermatologist or plastic surgeon were to examine you and tell you that your appearance is within the normal range and there's nothing significantly flawed about your face, would you be able to accept their professional assessment, or do you think you would still be convinced that there's something wrong with your appearance?\n\nPatient: I haven't really thought about consulting a specialist like a plastic surgeon or dermatologist. I'm honestly not sure if I would be able to believe them, because I feel so strongly that my face looks wrong. Even if they told me it was fine, I think I would still see the flaws when I look in the mirror.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your concerns about your appearance would decrease if you were to receive reassurance from multiple people, including professionals, that your appearance is normal, or would your concerns persist despite their reassurances?\n\nPatient: I already ask my little sister for reassurance constantly, but it never stops me from getting stuck in that loop and being late. Because I can see how crooked and swollen my nose is so clearly in the mirror, I don't think even a professional's reassurance would change how I feel. My concerns would definitely persist because the flaws are just too obvious to me.\n\nDoctor: Do you experience any other recurring, intrusive thoughts or compulsions to perform specific rituals outside of those related to your appearance, such as excessive cleaning, ordering, or counting?\n\nPatient: No, I don't experience anything like that. I've never had any urges to do things like excessive cleaning, ordering, or counting. My worries and rituals are strictly focused on my appearance and how my face looks.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how much time you spend each day thinking about your appearance or performing rituals to check or fix how you look?\n\nPatient: It takes up a massive portion of my day—honestly, it feels like pretty much all day because my brain constantly circles back to my face even when I'm working or talking to my mom. Before my shifts, I can spend hours stuck in that loop of bouncing between the mirror, taking selfies, and redoing my makeup. It takes so much time that I am repeatedly late for work because I just can't stop.\n\nDoctor: If you were to cover your mirrors at home and avoid taking selfies for a period, such as a week, do you think your concerns about your appearance would decrease, or would they persist even without the constant visual reminders?\n\nPatient: I think my worries would actually get worse because even without a mirror, my mind constantly circles back to how crooked and swollen my nose looks throughout the day. Not being able to check would make me feel completely out of control and terrified of what other people are seeing when they look at me.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that others notice the flaws in your appearance as readily as you do, or do you think they might not see them as clearly as you see them?\n\nPatient: I absolutely believe everyone notices it immediately. I constantly picture how awful my face looks to other people, especially under the bright store lights and security cameras at work. It feels like everyone can see that something is completely wrong with me the second they look up.\n\nDoctor: If you were to see a picture of yourself from a few years ago, when you felt less anxious about your appearance, would you still perceive the same flaws in that picture, or do you think your perception of those flaws has changed over time?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, to be honest, because I try to completely avoid looking at old photos of myself. I haven't really thought about how my perception might have changed over time, since I'm just so focused on how bad it feels right now.\n\nDoctor: If you were to see a picture of yourself that someone else took, without you being able to check or prepare your appearance beforehand, do you think the flaws you perceive would be as noticeable to you as they are when you're checking yourself in the mirror?\n\nPatient: Unprepared photos are actually my absolute worst nightmare, which is why I completely avoid letting anyone take pictures of me. When I do see photos of myself, like from work events, I scrutinize them intensely because my crooked nose and uneven face look incredibly obvious and terrible, especially since I couldn't control the angle or lighting.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever experience any moments where you are able to forget about or not think about your appearance, or is it a constant preoccupation for you throughout the day?\n\nPatient: No, it is a constant preoccupation pretty much all day long. Even when I'm trying to focus on ringing up customers at work or talking to my mom, my mind just keeps circling back to how crooked and swollen my nose looks and how uneven my face is. I constantly worry about how awful it must look to everyone under those bright store lights and security cameras.\n\nDoctor: If you were to watch a video of yourself from an outside perspective, without being able to control the camera angles or editing, do you think you would still perceive the same level of flaws in your appearance as you do when you're checking yourself in the mirror?\n\nPatient: Yes, I would definitely see the same flaws, and they would probably look even worse to me. That is actually one of my biggest fears, especially with the security cameras at work under those bright lights where I can't control the angle. I constantly worry about how crooked and swollen my nose or how uneven my face must look in those videos.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your preoccupation with your appearance and the rituals you perform to check and fix it are unreasonable or excessive, or do you believe they are justified given the flaws you perceive in your appearance?\n\nPatient: It is incredibly exhausting and frustrating to get stuck in these loops and constantly be late, but I genuinely believe the flaws on my face, like my crooked nose and uneven features, are very real and obvious. Because these flaws feel so unacceptable and noticeable to everyone, I feel completely justified and compelled to try to fix them before I can leave the house, even if it seems excessive to other people.\n\nDoctor: If you were to accept that your appearance is within the normal range, as a professional might assess, would you still feel the need to perform these checking and fixing rituals, or would that change your behavior?\n\nPatient: It is really hard for me to even imagine accepting my appearance as normal because my crooked nose and uneven face feel incredibly real and obvious to me. Even if a professional told me I looked fine, I would still feel an uncontrollable urge to keep checking and fixing in the mirror because I can't shake the fear of how I look under those bright store lights and security cameras. I just wouldn't feel safe leaving the house without trying to fix it first.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your concerns about your appearance would improve if you were able to stop the repetitive behaviors of checking and fixing, or do you believe these behaviors are necessary to manage your appearance concerns?"

It takes so much time that I am repeatedly late for work because I just can't stop.\n\nDoctor: If you were to cover your mirrors at home and avoid taking selfies for a period, such as a week, do you think your concerns about your appearance would decrease, or would they persist even without the constant visual reminders?\n\nPatient: I think my worries would actually get worse because even without a mirror, my mind constantly circles back to how crooked and swollen my nose looks throughout the day. Not being able to check would make me feel completely out of control and terrified of what other people are seeing when they look at me.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that others notice the flaws in your appearance as readily as you do, or do you think they might not see them as clearly as you see them?\n\nPatient: I absolutely believe everyone notices it immediately. I constantly picture how awful my face looks to other people, especially under the bright store lights and security cameras at work. It feels like everyone can see that something is completely wrong with me the second they look up.\n\nDoctor: If you were to see a picture of yourself from a few years ago, when you felt less anxious about your appearance, would you still perceive the same flaws in that picture, or do you think your perception of those flaws has changed over time?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, to be honest, because I try to completely avoid looking at old photos of myself. I haven't really thought about how my perception might have changed over time, since I'm just so focused on how bad it feels right now.\n\nDoctor: If you were to see a picture of yourself that someone else took, without you being able to check or prepare your appearance beforehand, do you think the flaws you perceive would be as noticeable to you as they are when you're checking yourself in the mirror?\n\nPatient: Unprepared photos are actually my absolute worst nightmare, which is why I completely avoid letting anyone take pictures of me. When I do see photos of myself, like from work events, I scrutinize them intensely because my crooked nose and uneven face look incredibly obvious and terrible, especially since I couldn't control the angle or lighting.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever experience any moments where you are able to forget about or not think about your appearance, or is it a constant preoccupation for you throughout the day?\n\nPatient: No, it is a constant preoccupation pretty much all day long. Even when I'm trying to focus on ringing up customers at work or talking to my mom, my mind just keeps circling back to how crooked and swollen my nose looks and how uneven my face is. I constantly worry about how awful it must look to everyone under those bright store lights and security cameras.\n\nDoctor: If you were to watch a video of yourself from an outside perspective, without being able to control the camera angles or editing, do you think you would still perceive the same level of flaws in your appearance as you do when you're checking yourself in the mirror?\n\nPatient: Yes, I would definitely see the same flaws, and they would probably look even worse to me. That is actually one of my biggest fears, especially with the security cameras at work under those bright lights where I can't control the angle. I constantly worry about how crooked and swollen my nose or how uneven my face must look in those videos.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your preoccupation with your appearance and the rituals you perform to check and fix it are unreasonable or excessive, or do you believe they are justified given the flaws you perceive in your appearance?\n\nPatient: It is incredibly exhausting and frustrating to get stuck in these loops and constantly be late, but I genuinely believe the flaws on my face, like my crooked nose and uneven features, are very real and obvious. Because these flaws feel so unacceptable and noticeable to everyone, I feel completely justified and compelled to try to fix them before I can leave the house, even if it seems excessive to other people.\n\nDoctor: If you were to accept that your appearance is within the normal range, as a professional might assess, would you still feel the need to perform these checking and fixing rituals, or would that change your behavior?\n\nPatient: It is really hard for me to even imagine accepting my appearance as normal because my crooked nose and uneven face feel incredibly real and obvious to me. Even if a professional told me I looked fine, I would still feel an uncontrollable urge to keep checking and fixing in the mirror because I can't shake the fear of how I look under those bright store lights and security cameras. I just wouldn't feel safe leaving the house without trying to fix it first.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your concerns about your appearance would improve if you were able to stop the repetitive behaviors of checking and fixing, or do you believe these behaviors are necessary to manage your appearance concerns?\n\nPatient: I feel like these behaviors are absolutely necessary because I physically cannot bring myself to leave the house or face the bright store lights and cameras without checking first. I have to try and make my face look \"less messed up\" before anyone sees me. Even though I know this cycle just makes me late and doesn't actually solve the problem, I feel completely unable to stop."
